newsitem.title: KENYA: Protests disrupt Nairobi for second straight day.
newsitem.headline: Protests disrupt Nairobi for second straight day.

text.p: Students demanding political reforms and the departure of President Daniel arap Moi clashed with police in Kenya's capital on Tuesday in a second straight day of protests.
But clashes were much lighter than on Monday and Kenyan opposition politician Richard Leakey said the Indian Ocean port of Mombasa was the next target for a drive for constitutional reforms.

"Moi must go. We want reforms," chanted hundreds of students from Kenya Polytechnic, ordered closed on Monday, as they built makeshift barricades on Haile Selassie Avenue, a major highway through Nairobi and only a block from the government centre.
They blocked traffic and tried to push their way back into their campus, held by riot police since authorities closed the polytechnic on Monday after hours of clashes with thousands of students.
Unrest on Tuesday morning waned and traffic returned to normal but in the afternoon about 300 students gathered on the avenue, stoned policemen and set ablaze several stalls before police moved in.
Riot police dispersed the students, arresting four of them, during 15 minutes of clashes before traffic could flow again.
In Kenya's Indian Ocean port of Mombasa, Moslem preacher Sheikh Balala, a fierce critic of Moi, said he would tour the city and visit schools on Tuesday after returning from two years in exile.
Balala returned to Kenya on Saturday from exile in Germany vowing to spearhead a reform campaign but he has proved more extreme than an opposition-backed committee organising protests since June.
"I don't recognise the forthcoming elections and I would rather voters burned their registration cards," Balala told 1,000 supporters at Sakina Mosque in Mombasa on Monday night.
Balala received a muted welcome on his return to his home city. Aides said plans for a rally on Tuesday were cancelled.

Opposition leaders said they did not organise the polytechnic unrest, which they said was a spontaneous protest in favour of reforms by students angered by a draft parliamentary bill allowing the expulsion of students who do not pay fees.
Leakey told Reuters on Tuesday that Mombasa, the centre of Kenya's coast tourism industry, would be the next focus of the opposition-backed drive for constitutional reforms before a general election.

Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party, said the National Convention Executive Committee (NCEC) behind the reform campaign since June sought government agreement by the end of July.
"The NCEC is coordinating...and Mombasa has been identified as the next major event," said Leakey, an NCEC member, Kenya's former wildlife guardian and a renowned palaeontologist.
"We are conscious that Mombasa could turn very violent and are very conscious of the consequences and would hope to reach an understanding with the government by the end of the month," he added.
"The reform movement including opposition parties is very clear on its position: mass action will be used on an escalating basis to bring about constitutional reform," Leakey said.
At least nine people were killed in Kenya on July 7 during the country's worst political violence in seven years when riot police broke up a day of demonstrations called by the NCEC.
The July 7 violence, which closed down Nairobi, was followed by several days of student unrest in the capital last week, prompting authorities to close indefinitely two universities.
The reforms demanded by the opposition before the elections would reduce the power of Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years.
